Abstract:
Endoscopic endonasal surgery (EES) has fundamentally changed the management of anterior skull base meningiomas by enabling access to many lesions through a direct minimally invasive corridor that avoids traditional transcranial exposure. Improvements in endoscopic optical technology, surgical instrumentation, and skull base reconstruction have steadily expanded the range of tumors that can be treated through an endonasal approach. Even so, EES is not appropriate for every lesion, making thoughtful patient selection and surgical team experience the most important determinants of surgical success. This review explores where EES fits in the contemporary management of anterior skull base meningiomas, including olfactory groove, tuberculum sellae, and planum sphenoidale meningiomas, with particular attention to its indications, limitations, and situations in which EES may not be appropriate. Evidence comparing endoscopic endonasal and transcranial approaches for anterior skull base meningiomas is reviewed, with attention to how tumor anatomy, oncologic objectives, and individual patient characteristics influence the choice of approach. A major consideration is how surgical morbidity can be minimized without compromising oncologic and safety outcomes. Current strategies to protect critical neurovascular structures, reduce the risk of cerebrospinal fluid leakage, and improve skull base durability, including advances in vascularized reconstruction techniques, are discussed. Emerging outcome data and the evolving learning curve associated with EES are also reviewed. Rather than presenting EES as a universal solution, the evidence points toward a patient-centered approach in which operative strategy and clinical decision making is guided by tumor characteristics, anatomy, and surgical goals.

item.title: PET Tumour Segmentation in Head and Neck Cancer: Reproducibility, Reader Dependence and Concordance with CT-Defined Tumour Volume in a 154-Patient Cohort.
item.dc:creator: Pirson AS, Delahaut G, Georis R, Deheneffe S, Van der Vorst S, Kudura K
item.description:
Authors: Pirson AS, Delahaut G, Georis R, Deheneffe S, Van der Vorst S, Kudura K

Published: 2026-Oct-05

Abstract:
Purpose: Volumetric PET biomarkers carry substantial prognostic value in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), yet their clinical implementation is hampered by segmentation heterogeneity. A fundamental and unresolved question is which segmentation method is most suitable for routine clinical use, both for a reader experienced in PET segmentation and for a reader without PET segmentation experience, such as an ENT surgeon or a radiation oncologist. This study addressed this question by assessing the intra- and interobserver reproducibility of four PET segmentation methods in MIM Maestro Software Version 7.4.2, identifying tumour-related determinants of variability, and examining concordance between PET-derived metabolic tumour volume (MTV) and CT-based gross tumour volume (GTV). Methods: Two readers with contrasting PET segmentation experience, a nuclear medicine physician experienced in PET segmentation (R1) and an ENT surgeon without prior PET segmentation training (R2), applied four methods to the primary tumours of 154 patients with HNSCC (oral cavity, oropharynx, hypopharynx or larynx) treated with definitive (chemo)radiotherapy between 2010 and 2021: fixed absolute thresholds at SUV 3.0 and 4.0, a relative threshold at 41% of the maximum standardised uptake value (SUVmax), and a gradient edge-detection algorithm (PET Edge+). R1 segmented twice with a washout of at least 4 weeks; R2 performed one session and delineated CT-GTV in the 85 patients whose PET/CT-derived CT served directly as the radiotherapy planning scan. The second session of R1 served as the reference for all interobserver and MTV-GTV analyses. Agreement was assessed by ICC (two-way mixed model), coefficient of variation, repeatability coefficient and Bland-Altman analysis; determinants of variability by a multivariable linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept per patient. Results: All four methods demonstrated excellent intraobserver (ICC 0.993 to >0.999) and interobserver (ICC 0.989-0.996) reproducibility. SUV3.0 generated significantly more relative error than SUV41% (β = +3.1%; 95% CI 0.89, 5.3). PET Edge+ was the only method for which a significant method × reader interaction was observed in this reader pair: the reader without PET segmentation experience generated more error than the reader experienced in PET segmentation (β = +7.1%; 95% CI 3.9, 10), an effect concentrated in smaller tumours (below approximately 15 mL); in the 85-patient GTV subset, where tumours were larger on average, the interobserver ICC for PET Edge+ was 0.997. Conclusions: All four methods provided excellent volumetric reproducibility within a single clinical software platform, but they differed in reader dependence and in agreement with CT-defined GTV. Rather than supporting a universal segmentation standard, these findings suggest that the method should be selected according to its intended application, pending multicentre confirmation.

Abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate (a) changes in caries experience, (b) changes in periodontal status, and (c) the need for dental extractions in a cohort of patients treated with radiotherapy (RT) and chemoradiotherapy (RTCT) for head and neck cancer (HNC). METHODS: This prospective cohort study was approved by the local Ethics Committee (Ref. 22858/18) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID: NCT04009161). The study population consisted of patients with HNC who, prior to RT, underwent a dental examination followed by the elimination of oral foci of infection and were then enrolled in a follow-up program. The primary outcome was oral health worsening, defined as the onset of severe periodontitis and/or a DMFt score ≥ 13. Oral cavity RT dose was obtained contouring the 'buccal mucosa' organ at risk (OAR). RESULTS: In total, 113 patients were included (median follow-up: 44.77 months). The sample mainly included oral, oropharyngeal, nasopharyngeal and laryngeal cancers (89/113, 78.8%). Salivary glands, hypopharynx and other sites accounted for a minority of the cases (24/113, 21.2%). Seventeen patients (34.7%) experienced worsening of oral health status over time, which was associated with smoking (OR = 4.7, 95% CI: 1.27-17.37; p = 0.02). The DMFt index increased (difference: 4.08; 95% CI: 1.60-6.56; p = 0.001), and this increase was associated with smoking (β = 2.05, 95% CI: 0.27-3.83; p = 0.02). Although worsening of periodontitis stage was not statistically significant (p = 0.35), localized deterioration was observed, with an increase in sites with PPD ≥ 5 mm (p = 0.02). Forty-nine patients (43.4%) experienced tooth loss. Mean tooth loss was 2.12 teeth per patient (p = 0.05), primarily due to caries (48.5%) and periodontitis (48.1%). Independent risk factors for tooth loss were age (p = 0.025) and an RT dose > 60 Gy to the 'buccal mucosa' OAR (p = 0.023). Authors: Wiedemeyer K, Ferreira I, Adams DJ, Brenn T
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193209
Published: 2026-Oct-04

Abstract:
Cutaneous sebaceous neoplasms are rare adnexal tumours differentiated towards sebaceous glands, spanning a biological spectrum from benign (sebaceous adenoma, sebaceoma, nevus sebaceus) to outright malignant (sebaceous carcinoma). Most tumours are sporadic and solitary, with a predilection for the head and neck of elderly adults, but a clinically important subset is observed in the setting of Lynch syndrome/Muir-Torre syndrome. Recent large-scale genomic and transcriptomic studies have provided insights into the pathogenesis of these unique neoplasms, revealing a genetically heterogeneous landscape shaped by mismatch repair deficiency, UV damage, and abnormalities in several other key signalling pathways. The inclusion of nevus sebaceus within the sebaceous tumour family in the WHO 5th Edition of Skin Tumours reflects a conceptual shift, recognising nevus sebaceus as a clonal, mutation-driven neoplasm and a precursor lesion for secondary tumour development.

item.title: Comparative Evaluation of Feature Selection Algorithms for Predicting Radiation-Induced Complications in Head and Neck Cancer Using Multimodal CT and MRI Radiomics.
item.dc:creator: Khajetash B, Deevband MR, Stokes WA, Tavakoli M
item.description:
Authors: Khajetash B, Deevband MR, Stokes WA, Tavakoli M
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193200
Published: 2026-Oct-03
PMID: 42882894



Abstract:
Head and neck cancer (HNC) presents a significant challenge due to its anatomic complexity and treatment-related complications such as sticky saliva and xerostomia, which critically impair patients' quality of life. Recent advancements in imaging technologies, using the concept of radiomics, offer promising approaches for predicting these complications and ultimately reducing their incidence. In this regard, robust feature selection is critical in radiomics-based predictive modeling due to the high dimensionality, redundancy, and instability of extracted imaging biomarkers. This study aims to evaluate nine distinct feature selection algorithms-Boruta, Kruskal, Recursive Maximum Relevance minimum redundancy (R-MRmr), Relief, Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE), Forward Selection (FS), Backward Elimination (BE), Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO), and Principal Component Analysis (PCA)-as a feature-transformation comparator for predicting sticky saliva and xerostomia in HNC patients using clinical, dosimetric, MRI and CT radiomics data. The study involved 250 HNC patients who underwent radiotherapy from three different institutions. From MRI and CT images, a total of 321 radiomic features (107 from each CT, T1, and T2-weighted MRI) along with 20 clinical and dosimetric features were extracted. The predictive robustness of feature selection methods was further evaluated across five machine-learning classifiers, including K-nearest neighbors (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), logistic regression (LR), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), were initially benchmarked using a common feature selection procedure, after which SVM was selected as the reference classifier for systematic comparison of the feature-reduction approaches. Model performance was assessed using metrics objectives such as Area Under the Curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Among the evaluated feature selection approaches, R-MRmr and Relief generally yielded better discrimination, although performance varied according to toxicity endpoint and imaging modality. The highest AUCs were 0.85 for early sticky saliva (R-MRmr, T1-weighted MRI), 0.96 for early xerostomia (R-MRmr, T1-weighted MRI), 0.65 for late sticky saliva (Relief, combined CT+T1+T2), and 0.88 for late xerostomia (Relief, T1-weighted MRI). T1-weighted MRI frequently provided better individual-modality performance, whereas combining all three imaging modalities did not consistently improve discrimination. These findings demonstrate that the choice of feature selection strategy and imaging modality can materially influence radiomics-based toxicity prediction.

item.title: Chk1/2 Inhibition by AZD7762 Enhances Andrographolide-Induced DNA Damage, Impairs DNA Repair, and Promotes Apoptosis in Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma CAL-33 Cells.
item.dc:creator: Singh S, Kartha A, Jaiswal A, Tailor D, Dhanalakshmi S
item.description:
Authors: Singh S, Kartha A, Jaiswal A, Tailor D, Dhanalakshmi S
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193199
Published: 2026-Oct-03
PMID: 42882893



Abstract:
Background: Andrographolide (AG), a diterpenoid lactone and a major constituent of Andrographis paniculata, has shown promising antiproliferative effect on diverse cancer cell lines, including head and neck cancer. However, a significant anti-proliferative effect is observed only at high micromolar concentrations. Further, AG has been shown to have poor oral bioavailability. Therefore, it is essential to consider mechanism-based combinations that could synergistically enhance the therapeutic potential of this compound so that efficacy can be achieved in concentrations that are systemically achievable. Objective: The present study is aimed to evaluate the anticancer effects and associated molecular alterations of an AG and Chk1/2 inhibitor combination in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (CAL-33) cells since the earlier studies have suggested ATM/ATR/Chk1/2-mediated activation of DNA damage checkpoints. Methods: Normal FHs74int cells and HNSCC cells (CAL-33 and FaDu) were used to assess cell proliferation and cell death. Cell cycle distribution and apoptosis were analyzed by flow cytometry and Acridine orange/EtBr, respectively, in CAL-33 cells. DNA damage in CAL-33 and FaDu cells was assessed by comet assay. Changes in the expression of proteins implicated in apoptosis, cell cycle progression, and DNA damage signaling were examined using Western blotting. Results: While AG did not show any significant changes in the growth or cell death of normal FHs74int cells, it strongly inhibited proliferation of HNSCC cells, concomitant with G2/M arrest and apoptosis. AG and AZD7762 showed an IC50 of 2.743 μM and 0.02600 μM, respectively, on cell proliferation in CAL-33 cells. Furthermore, AG caused an accumulation of intracellular ROS, which was inhibited by treatment with N-acetylcysteine. Chk1, Chk2 and γH2AX phosphorylation were induced in a dose-dependent manner by treatment with AG. The combination of AG with Chk1/2 inhibitor AZD7762 showed a synergistic effect in inhibiting cell proliferation with a CI of 0.4 through inhibition of DNA repair and premature mitotic entry, ultimately resulting in programmed cell death. Conclusions: These findings provide evidence that AG selectively targets DNA damage and repair in HNSCC CAL-33 cells via cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. Further, the anticancer potential of AG can be significantly enhanced by combination with the Chk1/2 inhibitor AZD7762, preventing repair of AG-induced DNA damage and amplifying checkpoint stress responses, resulting in enhanced apoptotic cell death. Together, these findings support the therapeutic potential of AG and highlight checkpoint kinase inhibition as a rational combination strategy for HNSCC treatment.

item.title: Second Primary Malignancies in Gastrointestinal Cancer Survivors: Epidemiology, Risk Factors, and Future Prediction Models.
item.dc:creator: Yadav J, Balizzakiwa T, Goyal H
item.description:
Authors: Yadav J, Balizzakiwa T, Goyal H
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193195
Published: 2026-Oct-03
PMID: 42882890



Abstract:
Advances in gastrointestinal (GI) cancer care have produced a growing population of long-term survivors at risk of second primary malignancies (SPMs). SPM definitions vary across studies, and SPMs remain underrepresented in cancer forecasting and prediction tools for GI cancer survivors. We conducted a narrative review across major GI cancer subtypes, summarizing site-specific SPM risk, key etiological pathways, and available prediction tools. Approximately one in ten colorectal cancer (CRC) survivors develops an SPM at ten years (pooled SIR ~1.15), a figure specific to CRC that does not generalize to other GI sites. Gastric cancer survivors carry excess risk of thyroid (O/E 2.00), esophageal, small intestinal, and pancreatic (O/E 1.60) malignancy, amplified by radiotherapy. Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma survivors show markedly elevated risk of upper aerodigestive tract tumors, consistent with field cancerization. Lynch syndrome (~16% second CRC risk at 10 years) and familial adenomatous polyposis (near-100% lifetime CRC risk without colectomy) confer some of the highest lifetime risks of metachronous GI malignancy reported to date. Most forecasting frameworks treat cancer incidence as a single event and do not adequately capture survivor-specific transitions, competing mortality, or germline susceptibility. GI cancer survivors form a distinct group whose risk is often overlooked. Harmonizing SPM definitions, extending multistate and competing-risk modeling, and integrating hereditary-risk stratification are near-term priorities for individualized surveillance.

item.title: Expression of Mitophagy-Associated Factors and Their Associations with Metastasis and Prognosis in Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Matsuzoe Y, Takeda D, Saito I, Murakami Y, Murakami A, Tadokoro Y, Hirota J, Kakei Y, Akashi M, Hasegawa T
item.description:
Authors: Matsuzoe Y, Takeda D, Saito I, Murakami Y, Murakami A, Tadokoro Y, Hirota J, Kakei Y, Akashi M, Hasegawa T
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193194
Published: 2026-Oct-03
PMID: 42882888



Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Mitophagy-associated factors have been implicated in tumor behavior and patient outcomes; however, their clinical significance depends on tumor type, stage, and microenvironmental context, and consistent conclusions remain lacking. We aimed to comprehensively assess the expression of mitophagy-associated factors in a moderate-sized cohort of patients with oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) and clarify their prognostic significance. METHODS: A retrospective cohort study included 197 patients with OSCC who underwent primary surgical resection between August 2013 and October 2018. Immunohistochemical expression of mitophagy-associated factors, including transcription factor EB (TFEB), nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2), activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4), Parkin, PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1), and mitochondrial ubiquitin ligase (MITOL), was evaluated. Associations between protein expression and clinicopathological parameters, local control, 5-year disease-specific survival (DSS), regional control, and distant metastasis were analyzed. RESULTS: High expression of NRF2 and TFEB was significantly related with decreased DSS, poor regional control, and increased distant metastasis. High ATF4 expression was associated with distant metastasis and showed no association with DSS. Parkin, PINK1, and MITOL showed no significant association with patient outcomes. Explanatory multivariable analysis showed associations between high TFEB expression, vascular invasion, extranodal extension, and disease-specific mortality. CONCLUSIONS: TFEB expression showed an exploratory association with aggressive tumor behavior and poor prognosis in OSCC, warranting further investigation. However, because immunohistochemical evaluation measures protein expression rather than mitophagy flux or mitochondrial turnover, these findings represent associations between mitophagy-associated factor expression and clinical outcomes and do not directly demonstrate altered mitophagy activity.

item.title: Self-management support interventions for patients with cancer treatment-related oral mucositis: a scoping review.
item.dc:creator: Yan H, Liu X, Li J, Ma D, Wang W, Xie Y, Wang L, Ning L
item.description:
Authors: Yan H, Liu X, Li J, Ma D, Wang W, Xie Y, Wang L, Ning L
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1950737
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42891185



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cancer treatment-related oral mucositis (OM) is one of the most common adverse effects of cancer treatment and can substantially impair patients' quality of life. Its effective management depends heavily on patients' continuous self-management. This scoping review aimed to systematically map the intervention components, delivery modes, and existing limitations of self-management support interventions, thereby providing evidence to inform the optimization of intervention strategies. METHODS: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews. Seven databases, including PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CINAHL, Embase, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, and WanFang, were searched from inception to May 10, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened titles, abstracts, and full texts according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were charted using a standardized form and summarized using descriptive numerical and content analyses. RESULTS: A total of 7,132 records were identified, and 16 studies were ultimately included, comprising 9 quasi-experimental studies, 6 randomized controlled trials, and 1 mixed-methods study. The interventions were primarily hospital-based and nurse-led, with some incorporating digital tools or written materials. Reported outcomes generally included OM-related clinical outcomes, quality of life, self-management-related outcomes, and nutritional status, although the direction and magnitude of findings varied across studies. CONCLUSIONS: Existing studies have reported potential improvements in OM-related and self-management-related outcomes following self-management support interventions. However, these findings should be interpreted cautiously because of heterogeneity in study designs, intervention components, and outcome measures, together with the absence of critical appraisal. Further well-designed studies using standardized outcome measures are needed to strengthen the evidence base.

item.title: Pretreatment body mass index as a prognostic factor for clinical course and survival in primary surgically treated oral squamous cell carcinoma - a retrospective study.
item.dc:creator: Floegel E, Brandenburg LS, Arias Romero JA, Vach K, Metzger MC, Schmelzeisen R, Wüster J
item.description:
Authors: Floegel E, Brandenburg LS, Arias Romero JA, Vach K, Metzger MC, Schmelzeisen R, Wüster J
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1894543
Published: 2026-01-01

Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: In oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), body mass index (BMI) is an available but imperfect marker of nutritional reserve. Evidence on pretreatment BMI in surgery-based European OSCC cohorts remains limited, especially regarding perioperative outcomes. This study evaluated associations of pretreatment BMI with overall survival (OS), recurrence-free survival (RFS), and perioperative outcomes after curative-intent R0 resection. METHODS: This retrospective single-center cohort included adult patients with previously untreated primary OSCC, available pretreatment BMI, and curative-intent R0 surgery between 2014 and 2023. BMI was assessed continuously and by World Health Organization (WHO) categories. OS and RFS were analyzed using multivariable Cox regression adjusted for age, sex, pathological T category, nodal status, microvascular free-flap reconstruction, and diabetes mellitus. Perioperative outcomes included red blood cell (RBC) transfusion, RBC units transfused, percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) placement, and intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital length of stay. RESULTS: A total of 274 patients with available pretreatment BMI were included; 116 deaths occurred. Five-year OS ranged from 31.4% in patients classified as underweight to 82.0% in patients with obesity. Higher BMI was associated with lower mortality (HR per 1 kg/m² 0.95, 95% CI 0.91-0.99; p = 0.013), and obesity was associated with improved OS compared with normal weight (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.26-0.96; p = 0.037). BMI was not significantly associated with RFS after adjustment (HR per 1 kg/m² 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.00; p = 0.080). Higher BMI was associated with fewer perioperative RBC transfusions (any transfusion: OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.84-0.98; p = 0.012; number of units: OR 0.89, 95% CI 0.82-0.95; p = 0.001). BMI was not independently associated with PEG placement or hospital length of stay; ICU findings depended on BMI modeling. DISCUSSION: Higher pretreatment BMI was associated with better OS and lower perioperative RBC transfusion requirements, whereas associations with RFS and most other perioperative outcomes were not significant after adjustment. Given the retrospective design and limitations of BMI as a body-composition marker, these findings should be interpreted cautiously. Pretreatment BMI may help identify low-BMI patients warranting early supportive-care assessment.

item.title: Integrated genome-wide DNA methylation and transcriptomic analysis prioritizes EPHA5 as a candidate non-invasive epigenetic biomarker for oral squamous cell carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Demokan S, Özemek B, Turna S, Cömert S, Şen C, Avcı K, Özkan A, Şen S, Poda M, Ulusan M, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Demokan S, Özemek B, Turna S, Cömert S, Şen C, Avcı K, Özkan A, Şen S, Poda M, Ulusan M, et al.
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1932336
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42890571



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) remains a major clinical challenge because of delayed diagnosis and the lack of validated non-invasive biomarkers for OSCC detection. Epigenetic alterations during oral carcinogenesis represent promising biomarker candidates. This study aimed to prioritize clinically relevant epigenetic biomarkers and validate EPHA5 using an integrated genome-wide DNA methylation and transcriptomic approach. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: Genome-wide DNA methylation and transcriptomic profiling were performed to identify epigenetically deregulated genes in OSCC. Candidate genes were prioritized by integrating DNA methylation, transcriptomic data and biological relevance. EPHA5 was subsequently selected for validation and evaluated by quantitative methylation-specific PCR (QMSP) and quantitative real-time PCR (QRT-PCR) in tissue, saliva and serum samples from independent cohorts comprising patients with OSCC, oral premalignant lesions (OPML) and healthy controls. RESULTS: Genome-wide analysis identified 661 upregulated and 577 downregulated genes together with 2,431 differentially methylated regions corresponding to 1,776 genes. Integrated analysis generated a panel of 51 candidate genes, from which EPHA5 was prioritized using integrated DNA methylation, gene expression, pathway enrichment and biological relevance. EPHA5 promoter hypermethylation was detected in 66.7% of OSCC tumors, whereas concurrent promoter hypermethylation and reduced expression were observed in 28.6% of tumors. Methylation was also detected in 54.5% of OPML lesions and in the saliva of 47.6% of OSCC patients but was rarely detected in healthy controls. Tumor EPHA5 methylation significantly discriminated OSCC from healthy controls (AUC = 0.780, p = 0.004; sensitivity, 71.4%; specificity, 75%). Salivary EPHA5 methylation also significantly discriminated OSCC from healthy controls (AUC = 0.717, p = 0.025; sensitivity, 52.4%; specificity, 87.5%), whereas serum methylation showed no significant diagnostic utility (AUC = 0.571, p = 0.462). Discrimination between OSCC and OPML was limited and did not reach statistical significance (tumor AUC = 0.662, p = 0.068; salivary AUC = 0.600, p = 0.264). CONCLUSIONS: Frequent tumor hypermethylation together with detectable salivary methylation supports further evaluation of EPHA5 as a candidate non-invasive epigenetic biomarker for OSCC. However, its moderate diagnostic performance, limited discrimination between OSCC and OPML, and lack of external validation indicate that larger prospective studies and evaluation within multimarker methylation panels are required before clinical implementation.

item.title: Same-Day Coordination of Mohs Surgery, Lymphoscintigraphy, and Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy for Merkel Cell Carcinoma: A Single-Center Feasibility Report.

Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193187
Published: 2026-Oct-02

Abstract:
Background/Objectives: Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is an aggressive neuroendocrine tumor, most commonly occurring on the head and neck. Incidence of MCC is rising with the aging population. Five-year overall survival (OS) for localized MCC is 50.6%; 5-year OS for patients with distant metastases is 13.5%. The purpose of this study is to determine if coordination of care for the treatment of MCC is logistically feasible, and provide a description of the patient population observed at this institution. Methods: All patients with MCC diagnosis from January 2012-June 2024 were identified at our tertiary care center. All patients with MCC were added to our non-melanoma skin cancer registry. Outcomes were compared between those treated with our "Merkel cell carcinoma in a day" (MIAD) protocol and those receiving the standard treatment protocol. Results: No significant differences were detected in the recurrence rate, transit metastasis, distant metastasis, and disease-specific death. Nodal metastasis was higher in the MIAD group (HR 4.94, 95% CI 1.08-22.6, p = 0.039, six events total). Both groups had similar times to treatment and treatment within 30 days of diagnosis. Conclusions: MCC is a rare and aggressive tumor, often exhibiting subclinical tumor spread. Mohs micrographic surgery ensures 100% peripheral and deep margin assessment, with potential for tissue sparing. With thoughtful coordination, lymphoscintigraphy can be completed on the same day as Mohs surgery followed by sentinel lymph node biopsy (SLNB) and reconstructive surgery.

Abstract:
BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Nasopharyngeal angiofibroma (NA) is generally benign, but recurrent disease and rare malignant transformation remain clinically relevant beyond adolescence. We examined adult clinical presentations, records of malignant transformation, and age-related differences in stage distribution. Radkowski stage distributions were compared between patients aged > 30 and ≤30 years using exact tests. Detailed clinical records were reviewed for 16 adults, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) annotation summaries were examined for one tumor-blood pair. In the detailed adult subgroup, a prior pathology-slide record described focal malignant transformation with a Ki-67 index of approximately 50% in one recurrent tumor. Two other patients had database transformation entries without accompanying pathological documentation. Four recurrences and three deaths were recorded, all in stage IIIB disease. Three men had colorectal or rectal cancer histories. Low-, intermediate-, and advanced-stage tumors accounted for 36.0%, 36.0%, and 28.0% of adult cases, compared with 17.6%, 57.3%, and 25.2% of younger cases (p = 0.0493). Abstract:
PURPOSE: TAPUR is a phase II basket trial evaluating the antitumor activity of commercially available targeted agents in patients with advanced cancer and genomic alterations. Results of two cohorts of patients with advanced thyroid (TC) or biliary tract cancer (BTC) with BRAF V600E mutations treated with cobimetinib plus vemurafenib (C + V) are reported. METHODS: Eligible patients had measurable disease (RECIST v1.1), Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status 0-2, adequate organ function, and no standard treatment options. The primary end point was disease control (DC), defined as objective response (OR) or stable disease (SD) of at least 16+ weeks duration. Simon's two-stage design was based on a null DC rate of 15% versus 35% (power = 0.85; α = .10). Both cohorts expanded to stage II but closed before reaching the target sample size by pharmaceutical company request; inferences are based on thresholds set forth in the protocol to maintain the α level. Secondary end points included OR, progression-free survival, overall survival, duration of response, duration of SD, and safety. RESULTS: Patients with TC (N = 22; n = 16 evaluable) or BTC (N = 18; n = 15 evaluable) with BRAF V600E mutations were enrolled. Twenty-one patients (53%) had ≥1 treatment-related grade 3 to 4 adverse event (AE) or serious AE. CONCLUSION: The combination of C + V met the prespecified criteria to declare a signal of activity in patients with TC and BTC with BRAF V600E mutations.

item.title: Preterm Risk Factors, Epigenetic Age, and Neurodevelopmental Outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Christensen R, Konwar C, Zhuang BC, MacIsaac J, Chau V, Cizmeci MN, Ly LG, Guo T, Branson H, Kobor MS, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Christensen R, Konwar C, Zhuang BC, MacIsaac J, Chau V, Cizmeci MN, Ly LG, Guo T, Branson H, Kobor MS, et al.

Abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Studies examining biological factors associated with neurodevelopment in the preterm population are limited. It was previously demonstrated that epigenetic age acceleration was associated with better neurodevelopmental outcomes among children born preterm. It is unclear whether this association is modified by clinical and environmental preterm risk factors. OBJECTIVE: To examine whether the association between epigenetic aging and neurodevelopmental outcomes is modified by preterm brain injury and socioeconomic status. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a prospective cohort study of children born at 24 to 32 weeks' gestation, recruited from 2 neonatal intensive care units from 2015 to 2019 and followed up to January 2026. The cohort was well characterized with clinical data, brain magnetic resonance imaging, and neurodevelopmental assessments (Bayley-III cognitive and motor domains) at 3 years. Participants with buccal epithelial cell DNA collected at 3 years were included. EXPOSURE: Epigenetic age (in weeks) at 3 years was determined using the pediatric buccal epigenetic clock and corrected for chronological age to give epigenetic age difference. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Primary analyses used linear regression to examine the association between epigenetic age difference, preterm risk factors (any brain injury, severe brain injury, maternal educational level), and cognitive and motor outcomes at 3 years. Secondary analyses examined whether brain injury and maternal education level modified the associations between epigenetic age difference and cognitive and motor outcomes at 3 years. RESULTS: A total of 102 study participants (median gestational age, 27.0 weeks [IQR, 25.6-28.9 weeks]; 54 female [53%]) were included. Higher maternal educational level (β = 11.65; 95% CI, 3.55-19.76; P = .005) and epigenetic age acceleration (β = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.14; P = .04) were associated with higher cognitive scores. Epigenetic age acceleration was also associated with higher motor scores (β = 0.16; 95% CI, 0.06-0.27; P = .003), while extreme prematurity (β = -5.66; 95% CI, -10.85 to -0.46; P = .03) and severe brain injury (β = -10.99; 95% CI, -21.32 to -0.66; P = .04) were associated with lower motor scores. Severe brain injury modified the association between epigenetic aging and motor outcomes (β = 0.41; 95% CI, 0.08-0.74; P = .02), and children with epigenetic age acceleration in the presence of severe brain injury had higher motor scores. CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: In this prospective preterm cohort study, epigenetic aging, severe brain injury, and socioeconomic status were associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes. Children with severe brain injury along with epigenetic age acceleration had higher motor scores. These findings suggest the association between epigenetic aging and neurodevelopment is context dependent and can vary based on the presence of preterm risk factors.

item.title: Epigenetic Priming with Oral Decitabine/Cedazuridine Combined with Nivolumab in Unresectable or Metastatic Mucosal Melanoma: Clinical and Correlative Findings from a Phase Ib/II Trial.
item.dc:creator: Borgers JSW, Wu CC, Medina TM, Muckle CM, Katsnelson EN, Whitty PA, Mantle L, Patel SP, Gao D, Jordan KR, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Borgers JSW, Wu CC, Medina TM, Muckle CM, Katsnelson EN, Whitty PA, Mantle L, Patel SP, Gao D, Jordan KR, et al.
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193172
Published: 2026-Oct-01
PMID: 42882866



Abstract:
Background/Objectives: Mucosal melanoma is a rare, aggressive melanoma subtype with lower response rates to immune checkpoint inhibitors than cutaneous melanoma. We previously identified reduced expression of innate immune pathogen-sensing pathway genes in mucosal melanoma, including components of the retinoic acid-inducible gene-I (RIG-I) pathway, and found that decitabine can induce re-expression of these immune genes and tumor-associated antigens. This study evaluated epigenetic immune priming with oral decitabine/cedazuridine (DEC-C) combined with nivolumab in patients with unresectable or metastatic mucosal melanoma. Methods: NCT05089370 was an open-label, single-center, single-arm phase Ib/II trial. Patients received DEC-C (35 mg decitabine/100 mg cedazuridine) orally for five days followed by nivolumab 480 mg every four weeks. The primary endpoint was safety and determination of the recommended phase II dose (RP2D). Secondary endpoints included objective response rate (ORR) and survival outcomes. Exploratory endpoints assessed immune and epigenetic correlates. Results: Eight patients were enrolled. Treatment-related adverse events occurred in seven patients (88%), with dose-limiting toxicities observed in three (38%). The RP2D was not established due to premature trial closure. At data cut-off, two patients remained on treatment with ongoing partial responses. The ORR was 25% (95% CI, 3.2-65), median progression-free survival was 3.0 months (95% CI, 2.1-not reached), and median overall survival was 7.2 months (95% CI, 4.4-not reached). Treatment significantly decreased global DNA methylation and induced RIG-I pathway genes in circulating immune cells. Conclusions: DEC-C plus nivolumab was associated with frequent treatment-related toxicities consistent with the known safety profiles of decitabine and nivolumab and demonstrated on-target epigenetic and immune activity in circulating cells. Although two partial responses were observed, the small sample size and wide confidence interval preclude conclusions regarding efficacy. These findings support future biomarker-integrated studies evaluating epigenetic immune-priming combinations in mucosal melanoma, with prospective optimization of dose, schedule, and treatment setting.

item.title: Preoperative Systemic Inflammatory Indices as Adjunctive Biomarkers for Malignancy Prediction in Bethesda III (AUS) Thyroid Nodules.
item.dc:creator: Baykal GR, Keskin M, Katipoğlu K, Dumlu EG, Özdemir D, Topaloğlu O, Ersoy R, Çakır B
item.description:
Authors: Baykal GR, Keskin M, Katipoğlu K, Dumlu EG, Özdemir D, Topaloğlu O, Ersoy R, Çakır B
Journal: Cancers | DOI: 10.3390/cancers18193170
Published: 2026-Oct-01
PMID: 42882864



Abstract:
Background/Objectives: Atypia of undetermined significance (AUS; Bethesda category III) remains a challenging thyroid cytological diagnosis because of its heterogeneous malignancy risk and limited preoperative certainty. Molecular testing can improve risk stratification but is not universally available. This study evaluated the diagnostic and incremental predictive value of preoperative complete blood count-derived systemic inflammatory indices in surgically treated Bethesda III thyroid nodules. Methods: This retrospective cohort included 352 patients who underwent thyroidectomy for Bethesda III thyroid nodules. Preoperative neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), systemic inflammation response index (SIRI), and aggregate index of systemic inflammation (AISI) were evaluated. Postoperative histopathology served as the reference standard. Receiver operating characteristic analysis and multivariable logistic regression were performed, followed by incremental model assessment, bootstrap internal validation, Hashimoto thyroiditis interaction analysis, and exploratory molecular subgroup analysis. Results: Among 352 patients, 197 (56.0%) had malignant histopathology. Malignant nodules showed higher NLR, PLR, SII, SIRI, and AISI and lower LMR. All six indices remained independently associated with malignancy after multivariable adjustment, with the strongest positive associations observed for SII (adjusted OR, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.60-2.72) and NLR (adjusted OR, 1.96; 95% CI, 1.51-2.54). SII demonstrated the numerically highest individual discrimination (AUC 0.687; 95% CI, 0.631-0.740), followed by NLR (AUC 0.661) and AISI (AUC 0.659); SII and NLR did not differ significantly (DeLong p = 0.182). Addition of SII increased the AUC of the clinico-ultrasonographic model from 0.695 to 0.761, with an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.721. Hashimoto thyroiditis did not significantly modify these associations. In the molecular subgroup, mutation status increased model discrimination from 0.765 to 0.824, whereas no statistically significant additional improvement with SII was detected in the exploratory molecular subgroup. Conclusions: Preoperative systemic inflammatory indices, particularly SII, provide modest but incremental predictive information beyond conventional clinical and ultrasonographic variables in surgically treated Bethesda III thyroid nodules. Their role appears complementary rather than diagnostic when used in isolation, particularly when comprehensive molecular testing is unavailable. Prospective external validation is required before clinical implementation.

item.title: Adipokine regulation of immune cell polarization in oral cancer and its impact on chemotherapy sensitivity.
item.dc:creator: Wang P, Qiao J, Qi J, Li H, Li J, Lin K, Chang B
item.description:
Authors: Wang P, Qiao J, Qi J, Li H, Li J, Lin K, Chang B
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1954382
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42877600



Abstract:
Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the most common malignant tumor in the head and neck region. In locally advanced patients, neoadjuvant chemotherapy centered on cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil often leads to primary/acquired resistance, with a 5-year survival rate of less than 50%. Tumor microenvironment (TME) immunosuppressive remodeling is the core cause of chemotherapy failure. Adipokines secreted by cancer-associated adipocytes (CAAs) are the key mediators that link metabolic disorders, immune polarization and chemotherapy resistance. The adipokines leptin, adiponectin, chemerin, resistin, and GDF15 signal through pathways such as JAK2/STAT3, PI3K/AKT, NF-κB, and PPARγ to bidirectionally regulate the polarization phenotypes of tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs), myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), CD4+/CD8+ T cells, and NK cells. Pro-cancer adipokines induce M2-type TAMs, MDSCs expansion, Th2/Th17 polarization, and effector T cell exhaustion, constructing an immunosuppressive microenvironment, upregulating DNA damage repair, drug efflux, and anti-apoptotic genes, and reducing cisplatin/5-FU chemosensitivity. The tumor-suppressive adipokine adiponectin promotes M1 macrophage and CD8+ effector T cell infiltration, reverses immunosuppression, and sensitizes chemotherapy. This article systematically reviews the origin and classification of adipokines, the polarization patterns of immune cells in the OSCC microenvironment, the molecular pathways by which various adipokines regulate immune polarization, and the complete mechanism by which immune polarization mediates chemotherapy resistance. It summarizes the value of clinical markers and targeted reversal strategies, points out current research bottlenecks, and looks forward to the translational prospects of metabolism-immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy, aiming to provide new metabolism-immune targets for overcoming chemotherapy resistance in oral cancer.

item.title: Potential involvement of a TLR4-associated CD155/TIGIT pathway in Porphyromonas gingivalis-induced immunosuppressive microenvironment formation in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Tian X, Xu L, Fu Y, Qiang Q, Cao X, Wang J, Liu L, Ling B
item.description:
Authors: Tian X, Xu L, Fu Y, Qiang Q, Cao X, Wang J, Liu L, Ling B
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1773440
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876819



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Accumulating evidence indicates that oral microbiota dysbiosis and periodontal pathogens contribute to the initiation and progression of oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC). However, the molecular mechanisms underlying the interaction between Porphyromonas gingivalis and the tumor immune microenvironment remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate the potential role of a TLR4-associated ERK/CD155/TIGIT signaling pathway in P. gingivalis-mediated immunosuppressive microenvironment formation during OSCC progression. METHODS: Genes associated with P. gingivalis and TIGIT were obtained from GeneCards and The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) databases. Candidate hub genes were identified through bioinformatic analyses. An SCC7 syngeneic orthotopic transplantation mouse model was established, and SCC7 cells were injected together with Porphyromonas gingivalis. Tumor growth was assessed by measuring tumor volume and weight. Expression levels of TLR4, ERK1/2, CD155, and TIGIT were evaluated by immunohistochemistry and quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR). Flow cytometry was performed to analyze tumor-infiltrating immune-cell populations. The TLR4 inhibitor TAK-242 was used to investigate the involvement of TLR4-associated signaling. RESULTS: Bioinformatic analysis identified TLR4 as a biologically relevant candidate hub gene potentially linking P. gingivalis-associated signaling and TIGIT-related immune regulation. Exposure to P. gingivalis significantly promoted tumor growth and increased the expression of TLR4, ERK1/2, CD155, and TIGIT in tumor tissues. Flow cytometric analysis revealed immune microenvironment remodeling characterized by increased proportions of CD4+ T cells, TIGIT-positive Tregs, and IL-10-positive cells, accompanied by reduced CD8+ T-cell infiltration and decreased frequencies of Ki67+CD8+ and CD44+CD8+ T cells. Treatment with the TLR4 inhibitor TAK-242 partially reversed these tumor-promoting, immunological, and molecular changes. CONCLUSION: Our findings suggest that exposure to P. gingivalis may promote OSCC progression by contributing to immune microenvironment remodeling. Increased expression of TLR4, ERK1/2, CD155, and TIGIT, together with the effects of TLR4 inhibition, supports the potential involvement of a TLR4-associated ERK/CD155/TIGIT signaling pathway in this process. However, the precise molecular mechanisms require further validation using genetic and functional approaches.

item.title: Preoperative biopsy underestimates tumour budding but retains prognostic value in oral squamous cell carcinoma.
item.dc:creator: Riese J, Cacchi C, Peppler J, Bonni G, Pannhausen J, Klein A, Müller-Diesing F, Jonigk D, Hölzle F, Klein M
item.description:
Authors: Riese J, Cacchi C, Peppler J, Bonni G, Pannhausen J, Klein A, Müller-Diesing F, Jonigk D, Hölzle F, Klein M
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1932265
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876767



Abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tumour budding is an established prognostic marker in oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC), but its reliability and prognostic performance in preoperative biopsy specimens remain uncertain. This study compared tumour budding assessment in matched biopsy and resection specimens and evaluated their respective prognostic value. METHODS: We retrospectively analysed 256 patients with OSCC and matched preoperative biopsy and resection specimens. Tumour budding at the invasive front was assessed on hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections according to the International Tumour Budding Consensus Conference criteria and agreement between biopsy- and resection-based assessment was evaluated alongside associations with clinicopathological characteristics, disease-specific survival and occult nodal metastasis using logistic regression and Cox proportional hazards models. RESULTS: Biopsy-derived tumour budding showed only weak correlation with resection findings and systematically underestimated high tumour budding, resulting in poor categorical agreement (κ = 0.11) and low sensitivity (9.8%) despite high specificity (98.9%). Nevertheless, both biopsy- and resection-based tumour budding were associated with disease-specific survival when mutually adjusted for each other. The C-index was numerically higher for resection-based than biopsy-based assessment (0.72 vs. 0.60), with only a modest increase when both measures were combined (C-index 0.74). Both biopsy- and resection-derived tumour budding were also associated with local recurrence and distant metastasis in mutually adjusted Cox models, although these secondary analyses remain exploratory. Interpretation is limited by the small biopsy high-budding group (n = 10) and the limited number of events for several secondary outcomes. For later lymph-node metastasis, only resection-derived tumour budding remained statistically significant after mutual adjustment, whereas the association with biopsy-derived tumour budding was borderline. Resection-derived tumour budding, but not biopsy-derived tumour budding, remained associated with occult nodal metastasis after mutual adjustment, while no statistically significant specimen-type interactions were detected for the evaluated clinicopathological characteristics, with several estimates remaining imprecise. DISCUSSION: Preoperative biopsy-derived tumour budding may provide clinically relevant prognostic information in OSCC despite systematically underestimating high tumour budding. Although resection-based assessment showed a numerically higher C-index, biopsy assessment may provide complementary preoperative prognostic information but should not be considered a surrogate for resection-based assessment.

item.title: Two-year dynamic risk stratification and adjuvant radioiodine efficacy in initial non-distant metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma harboring TERT promoter mutations.
item.dc:creator: Deng XZ, Liu MY, Shen CT, Song HJ, Wang J, Fan YB, Luo QY, Tang J, Wei XE, Qiu ZL
item.description:
Authors: Deng XZ, Liu MY, Shen CT, Song HJ, Wang J, Fan YB, Luo QY, Tang J, Wei XE, Qiu ZL
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1895987
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876643



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: The clinical utility of postoperative radioiodine (131I) ablation remains unclear for patients with initially diagnosed non-distant metastatic papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) with harboring TERT promoter(TERT-p) mutations, it is unknown whether 131I therapy reduces the risk of persistent or recurrent disease. This study investigated clinicopathological features, 2-year dynamic therapeutic responses and progression-free survival (PFS) in this specific patient cohort. METHODS: A single-center retrospective cohort study enrolled 113 eligible patients, allocated to the 131I ablation group (n=62) and non-131I group (n=51). Two-year dynamic risk stratification assessed treatment response. Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox regression models were used for survival analysis. RESULTS: The predominant TERT-p variant was C228T (89.4%), and most patients carried concurrent BRAFV600E mutations. Only initial surgical approach remained an independent intergroup variable. Within 2 years, 46.0% achieved acceptable responses, associated with sex and primary surgery (p=0.036,p < 0.001). High baseline ATA risk was strongly correlated with structural residual lesions and unfavorable therapeutic response (p < 0.001).No significant between-group differences in response were observed across all ATA risk subgroups. The median follow-up was 4.6 years; 3- and 5-year PFS rates were 67.5% and 39.1%. Age ≥55 years, N1b stage and high baseline ATA risk were independent adverse predictors of PFS. Both 2-year therapeutic response and PFS at the end of follow-up exhibited no statistical differences between the 131I group and non-131I group. CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective observational cohort, postoperative 131I ablation was not associated with improved PFS among patients with non-distant metastatic TERT-p-mutant PTC. Advanced age, N1b lymphatic metastasis and high baseline ATA risk independently predict poor outcomes. Biologically, TERT-p mutations induce tumor dedifferentiation and impaired iodine uptake, diminishing 131I efficacy. Clinically, routine 131I yields no survival benefit for this high-risk molecular subgroup, guiding individualized surveillance and avoiding redundant 131I exposure.

item.title: Time-segmented, feedback-guided tiered warming during radical esophagectomy: a single-center retrospective cohort study.
item.dc:creator: Liu Y, Ren J, Xiao L, Wang J, Wang L, Yi Y, Cheng J, Hu M
item.description:
Authors: Liu Y, Ren J, Xiao L, Wang J, Wang L, Yi Y, Cheng J, Hu M
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1920051
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876635



Abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether a protocolized intraoperative temperature-management strategy based on time-segmented warning thresholds and tiered, feedback-guided warming interventions reduces hypothermia and improves early postoperative recovery in patients undergoing radical esophagectomy. METHODS: This single-center retrospective comparative cohort study included 116 adults who underwent elective radical esophagectomy at The affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University between August 2024 and January 2026 and were managed with either a time-segmented, feedback-guided tiered warming protocol (n = 58) or conventional warming (n = 58). Core temperature was monitored continuously with a lower esophageal probe until the start of esophageal mobilization and with a nasopharyngeal probe thereafter, and was recorded every 15 min. All warming adjustments were implemented manually by the clinical team according to predefined thresholds. The primary endpoint was intraoperative hypothermia, defined as a core temperature below 36 °C at any time from incision to skin closure. Secondary endpoints included severe hypothermia, nadir temperature, hypothermia burden, postoperative shivering, time to extubation, post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) recovery time, coagulation indices, 30-day complications, length of stay, and hospital cost. RESULTS: Intraoperative hypothermia occurred in 53 of 58 control patients (91.4%) and 5 of 58 intervention patients (8.6%) (risk ratio 0.09, 95% CI 0.04-0.22; P < 0.001). Severe hypothermia below 35.5 °C developed in 27 control patients (46.6%) and in none of the intervention patients. Median nadir core temperature was 35.55 °C in the control group and 36.27 °C in the intervention group (P < 0.001). Compared with conventional warming, the protocol reduced postoperative shivering (5.2% vs 51.7%), shortened time to extubation by 8.9 min, lowered the rate of any postoperative complication (34.5% vs 62.1%; P = 0.005), shortened hospital stay (12.2 vs 13.5 days; P = 0.010), and reduced mean in-hospital cost by 8,911 CNY (P < 0.001). The treatment effect was materially unchanged in adjusted analyses using Firth penalized logistic regression (adjusted odds ratio 0.004, 95% CI 0.000-0.024) and modified Poisson regression (adjusted risk ratio 0.10, 95% CI 0.04-0.23). CONCLUSION: In adults undergoing radical esophagectomy, a time-segmented, feedback-guided tiered warming protocol substantially reduced intraoperative hypothermia and was associated with faster early recovery, fewer postoperative complications, shorter hospitalization, and lower cost. Because the intervention was a multicomponent warming bundle, the contributions of its individual components cannot be separated, and the associations with complications, hospital stay, and cost should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. The protocol uses standard perioperative equipment and can be implemented without specialized hardware.

item.title: Preparedness for early detection of oral cancer and oral potentially malignant disorders among Saudi dental students: a multicenter cross-sectional survey.
item.dc:creator: Tarakji B, Alsalhani A, Mehsen Alali F, Alqhtani NR, Alqahtani AS, Bin Nabhan A, Almansour A, Alrubayyi A, Kariri M, Alshahrei MS, et al.
item.description:
Authors: Tarakji B, Alsalhani A, Mehsen Alali F, Alqhtani NR, Alqahtani AS, Bin Nabhan A, Almansour A, Alrubayyi A, Kariri M, Alshahrei MS, et al.
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1914773
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876606



Abstract:
BACKGROUND: Oral cancer remains a major global health challenge, with delayed diagnosis contributing to poor prognosis and reduced survival. Dental students play an important role in early detection; however, deficiencies in preparedness and diagnostic confidence have been reported. This study assessed oral cancer knowledge, oral potentially malignant disorder (OPMD) awareness, and diagnostic confidence among Saudi dental students. METHODS: A quantitative cross-sectional online survey was conducted among 354 dental students and interns from governmental and private dental schools in Saudi Arabia. The questionnaire assessed oral cancer knowledge, OPMD knowledge, and self-reported diagnostic confidence related to screening and biopsy procedures. Participants were classified as meeting or not meeting a study-defined minimum operational threshold of ≥60% of the maximum possible score in each domain; this cutoff was not interpreted as a definition of "good" performance or clinical competence. Associations between participant characteristics and study outcomes were examined using chi-square tests and multivariable binary logistic regression analyses. RESULTS: Overall, 81.9% of participants met the oral cancer knowledge threshold, 55.4% met the OPMD knowledge threshold, and 24.0% met the diagnostic confidence threshold. Most participants correctly identified major oral cancer risk factors, including tobacco smoking (97.2%), alcohol consumption (92.7%), and human papillomavirus infection (86.7%). However, clinically oriented response patterns highlighted areas for educational attention. 20.1% selected the prespecified specialist-referral response for management of a persistent suspicious lesion, while 35.6% recognized factors associated with increased malignant transformation risk in leukoplakia. Intern status remained independently associated with meeting the oral cancer knowledge and diagnostic confidence thresholds in multivariable analyses. The diagnostic-confidence outcome reflected self-perceived preparedness rather than observed screening, referral, or procedural competence. CONCLUSION: A high proportion of Saudi dental students met the study-defined oral cancer knowledge threshold; however, self-reported diagnostic confidence and preparedness for early detection remained considerably lower. Strengthening competency-based oral cancer education and clinical training may improve early detection preparedness and referral practices among future dental practitioners. Because the domains assessed different constructs and had different effective cutoffs, their threshold proportions should not be compared directly; the diagnostic-confidence findings represent perceived preparedness only.

item.title: Clinical outcomes after reirradiation with dose painting of recurrent or second primary head and neck cancer.
item.dc:creator: Dale E, Evensen ME, Amdal CD, Furre T, Moan JM, Heggebø LC, Løndalen AM, Malinen E
item.description:
Authors: Dale E, Evensen ME, Amdal CD, Furre T, Moan JM, Heggebø LC, Løndalen AM, Malinen E
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1966123
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876552



Abstract:
PURPOSE: Recurrent or second primary head and neck cancer (rsHNC) presents a radiotherapeutic challenge due to limited tolerance of previously irradiated tissues. These patients could benefit from dose painting (DP), which focuses on delivering maximal dose to areas of high tumor burden while respecting dose constraints to organs at risk. In this study, we compare clinical outcomes in one group receiving standard reirradiation with a group receiving 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) PET/CT-guided DP. METHODS: Our standard reirradiation regimen is hyperfractionated radiotherapy (RT) of 1.5 Gy x 40 (60 Gy total dose). For DP, we defined two FDG-based prescription volumes receiving at least 65 Gy and 70 Gy. Thirteen patients receiving standard RT were compared with 10 DP patients. Toxicity was scored using CTCAE v3.0. Disease-related endpoints were locoregional control (LRC), disease-free survival (DFS) and overall survival (OS). RESULTS: The mean composite toxicity score was maximal at the end of RT, with varying patterns across the CTCAE items. No significant difference in toxicity was found between the groups except for dysphagia at 6 months, where the standard RT group had worse scores (p=0.01). No differences were found in LRC and DFS. Two-year OS was 50% in the DP group versus 15% in the standard group (p=0.04), although this may reflect higher comorbidity in the standard group. CONCLUSION: DP of rsHNC did not increase toxicity compared with standard reirradiation. No evidence of improved disease control was found. However, DP may benefit selected patients, and future studies should focus on identifying these candidates. CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: https://clinicaltrials.gov, identifier NCT02921581.

item.title: Local control after stereotactic radiation for thyroid cancer: a histology risk-stratified analysis.
item.dc:creator: Gui B, Sekar J, Locke M, Saha S, Tulchinsky M, Jones B, Seetharamu N, Ghaly M
item.description:
Authors: Gui B, Sekar J, Locke M, Saha S, Tulchinsky M, Jones B, Seetharamu N, Ghaly M
Journal: Frontiers in oncology | DOI: 10.3389/fonc.2026.1898567
Published: 2026-01-01
PMID: 42876475



Abstract:
PURPOSE/OBJECTIVES: Recurrent and metastatic non-anaplastic thyroid cancer has traditionally been considered relatively radioresistant. We evaluated whether anatomic site or histology risk group better predicts local control (LC) following stereotactic radiation therapy (SBRT/SRS). MATERIALS/METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed 32 patients with 66 treated lesions (42 skeletal, 24 non-skeletal) treated between 2012 and 2025. Histology was dichotomized into low-risk (papillary, follicular, medullary, Hürthle cell; n=61) and high-risk (poorly differentiated and squamous cell carcinoma; n=5). BED10 was calculated using α/β = 10 Gy. LC was defined per RECIST 1.1. Kaplan-Meier and log-rank tests were used. Intra-patient correlation was addressed via generalized estimating equations (GEE) and Cox shared frailty models. A multivariable GEE model included histology risk, site, BED10, PTV volume, prior surgery, and age. RESULTS: Median follow-up was 15.0 months. Six local failures occurred (crude LC 90.9%); 1- and 2-year LC were 96.5% and 87.1%. Histology risk was the dominant determinant: low-risk histology achieved 95.1% crude LC versus 40.0% for high-risk (log-rank p=0.002). In multivariable GEE analysis, low-risk histology was independently associated with LC (OR 158.0, 95% CI 1.72-14,479.7; p=0.028), whereas skeletal site was not (OR 1.07, 95% CI 0.02-51.8; p=0.974). BED10 was not associated with LC after adjustment (p=0.752). Skeletal and non-skeletal LC were similar after histology stratification (95.0% vs 95.2% among low-risk). Treatment was well tolerated; no Grade ≥3 radiation toxicity, myelopathy, or fractures occurred. CONCLUSION: In stereotactic radiation for metastatic non-anaplastic thyroid cancer, histology risk grouping-not anatomic site or dose escalation-is the dominant predictor of local control. These findings support histology-based risk stratification for SRT patient selection.
